questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Society Builds Support Services' refers to.
questions.a: A family, though the basic unit of society, cannot deliver every specialised need of its members -- schooling, hospitals, training and recreation -- so communities raise extra structures, and the state steps in further where poverty or separation leaves members unable to cope.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Society Builds Support Services'.
questions.a: With about a third of the world's poor living in India, state programmes and NGO effort must backstop struggling families.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Why Society Builds Support Services', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: need chain -- family plus community structures plus state institutions cover member needs

concepts.title: Vulnerability of Children, Youth and Elderly

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Vulnerability of Children, Youth and Elderly' refers to.
questions.a: A person or group is vulnerable when adverse circumstances strike harder and more often; children qualify because rapid, interconnected development stalls when food, health, love and stimulation are missing, and youth and the elderly qualify through the special pressures and losses of their stages.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Vulnerability of Children, Youth and Elderly'.
questions.a: Two thirds of under fives face moderate or severe malnutrition, three million children live on the streets, and 17 million children work by official count.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Vulnerability of Children, Youth and Elderly', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: vulnerability = unmet needs multiplied by stage specific exposure

concepts.title: Juvenile Justice Act and Children in Need

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Juvenile Justice Act and Children in Need' refers to.
questions.a: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act of 2000, India's first juvenile justice framework, separates children who clash with the law from those needing care and protection -- the abandoned, the abused, the trafficked, disaster victims and others -- and demands a child friendly approach for their rehabilitation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Juvenile Justice Act and Children in Need'.
questions.a: The Act aligns with the Child Rights Convention and lists exactly which children count as needing care and protection.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Juvenile Justice Act and Children in Need', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: two categories -- in conflict with law plus in need of care and protection

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'ICDS and the Anganwadi' refers to.
questions.a: The Integrated Child Development Services, the largest early childhood programme anywhere, bundles health, nutrition, stimulation and early learning for children under six with education for mothers, immunisation and growth monitoring, all delivered through the neighbourhood anganwadi centre.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'ICDS and the Anganwadi'.
questions.a: Over 41 million children are covered; non formal preschool runs for the three to six band and supplementary feeding for all under six.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'ICDS and the Anganwadi', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: integrated bundle -- health plus nutrition plus preschool plus immunisation through one centre

concepts.title: SOS Children's Villages and Children's Homes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'SOS Children's Villages and Children's Homes' refers to.
questions.a: SOS Children's Villages give orphaned and abandoned children a trained mother, ten to fifteen siblings and a family style home clustered into a village, while the state runs observation homes for investigation stays, special homes for juveniles found guilty and children's homes for those with no traceable family.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'SOS Children's Villages and Children's Homes'.
questions.a: The first Indian SOS village opened in 1964; today about 6000 children live across 40 villages, and emergency relief after disasters often becomes permanent village capacity.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'SOS Children's Villages and Children's Homes', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: care ladder -- SOS family home to observation home to special home to children's home

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Adoption and CARA' refers to.
questions.a: Adoption in India moved from a family bound religious practice to an institutionalised legal route; the Central Adoption Resource Authority, created on the Supreme Court's advice, writes the guidelines that guard the welfare and rights of adopted children, with NGOs running the delivery systems.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Adoption and CARA'.
questions.a: CARA exists to strengthen adoption rules and protect the child's interests.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Adoption and CARA', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: adoption route -- policy plus CARA guidelines plus NGO delivery

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Youth Vulnerability and Needs' refers to.
questions.a: The National Youth Policy of 2014 places youth in the fifteen to twenty nine band, with adolescents at thirteen to nineteen; the stage strains under body changes, livelihood and marriage preparation, competition and peer pressure, and can slide into substance abuse, with rural, tribal, out of school, female, disabled and trafficked youth most exposed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Youth Vulnerability and Needs'.
questions.a: Youth need education, training, jobs, shelter, health services, protection from exploitation and a voice in decisions that concern them.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Youth Vulnerability and Needs', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: age bands -- adolescents 13 to 19, youth 15 to 29

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Youth Programmes in India' refers to.
questions.a: Government channels youth energy through the National Service Scheme for college volunteers, the National Service Volunteer Scheme with Nehru Yuva Kendras for rural non student youth, adventure promotion, Scouts and Guides, the Commonwealth Youth Programme with its Chandigarh centre, and integration visits between states.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Youth Programmes in India'.
questions.a: The National Youth Policy was adopted in 2003 by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports; Kendra activities build literacy, self reliance and scientific temper among rural youth.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Youth Programmes in India', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: programme set -- NSS plus NSVS plus adventure plus scouts plus Commonwealth plus integration

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Elderly Vulnerability in India' refers to.
questions.a: India counts senior citizens from sixty years; falling physiological reserves bring illness and disabilities like cataract, deafness and arthritis, while children moving away, city fragmentation of families, financial dependence and rising living costs leave many elders lonely and unsupported.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Elderly Vulnerability in India'.
questions.a: Eighty per cent of the elderly live in villages, thirty per cent are below the poverty line, and most sixty plus Indians still work; the National Policy for Older Persons arrived in 1999.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Elderly Vulnerability in India', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: risk stack -- health decline plus isolation plus money dependence

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Programmes for the Elderly' refers to.
questions.a: Public and voluntary effort runs old age homes, respite and continuous care homes, multi service day centres, mobile medicare units for remote areas, dementia day care, help lines, mental health and physiotherapy services, caregiver training, awareness drives and the National Old Age Pension Scheme for destitute persons above sixty five.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Programmes for the Elderly'.
questions.a: NOAPS pension reaches destitute seniors over sixty five who must prove age and destitution, and states may top up the amount.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Programmes for the Elderly', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: programme set -- shelter plus health plus counselling plus pension plus awareness

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Managing Institutions and Programmes' refers to.
questions.a: Running a service organisation calls for people skills -- community ownership through participatory planning, private sector partnership, government liaison and harmonious internal relations -- plus administrative grip on finance, recruitment, records and equipment, all steered by a personal vision for the target group.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Managing Institutions and Programmes'.
questions.a: Programmes planned with the community from the start earn the ownership that keeps them alive.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Managing Institutions and Programmes', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: manager profile -- people skills plus administrative skills plus vision

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Career Routes in Support Services' refers to.
questions.a: Entry runs through an undergraduate degree in Home Science, Social Work or allied social sciences, with IGNOU and state open universities adding a certificate in NGO management or a diploma in youth development work; careers open as founder of one's own institution, manager of an established one, functionary at any cadre, or researcher evaluating programmes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Career Routes in Support Services'.
questions.a: Distance learning can run alongside a regular degree to build the specialised knowledge base.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Career Routes in Support Services', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: route -- degree plus open university courses to founder or manager or functionary or researcher

questions.q: Compute the average village load when the total children and the number of villages are stated. Use the method 'SOS Village Capacity Arithmetic'. Work with: total_children = 3, village_count = 10. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of children_per_village.
questions.a: 0.3 years

questions.q: Find the mean number of children per village from the network's totals. Use the method 'SOS Village Capacity Arithmetic'. Work with: total_children = 40, village_count = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of children_per_village.
questions.a: 0.8 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'SOS Village Capacity Arithmetic' refers to.
questions.a: When a network states its total child count and its number of villages, the average load per village is the total divided by the count of villages.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'SOS Village Capacity Arithmetic'.
questions.a: About 6000 children across 40 villages puts roughly 150 children in each village, housed in family homes of ten to fifteen.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'SOS Village Capacity Arithmetic', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: children_per_village = total_children / village_count

questions.q: Compute the gain in life expectancy when the historical and current figures are given. Use the method 'Life Expectancy Gain'. Work with: current_expectancy = 240, past_expectancy = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of expectancy_gain.
questions.a: 165 units

questions.q: Work out the improvement in years of life from the two expectancy values. Use the method 'Life Expectancy Gain'. Work with: current_expectancy = 60, past_expectancy = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of expectancy_gain.
questions.a: 42 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Life Expectancy Gain' refers to.
questions.a: The rise in how long people live is the difference between the current expectancy figure and the historical one, and that gain is what swells the elderly population the chapter describes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Life Expectancy Gain'.
questions.a: Expectancy climbed from about 29 years in 1947 to 69.3 years for females and 65.8 for males in 2009-13.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Life Expectancy Gain', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: expectancy_gain = current_expectancy - past_expectancy

questions.q: Using the method 'Elderly Population Shares', work with: share_pct = 0.8, total_elderly = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of elderly_count.
questions.a: 2.4 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Elderly Population Shares' and work with: share_pct = 0.5, total_elderly = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of elderly_count.
questions.a: 0.2 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Elderly Population Shares' refers to.
questions.a: Applying a stated percentage to the total elderly count prices each feature of the group: the village dwelling share, the poverty line share or any other quoted fraction becomes an absolute number of persons.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Elderly Population Shares'.
questions.a: Eighty per cent rural and thirty per cent poor are the two big shares to convert into head counts.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Elderly Population Shares', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: elderly_count = total_elderly * share_pct / 100

questions.q: Calculate the percentage of entrants who persist when the intake and the survivors are stated. Use the method 'School Retention Rate'. Work with: enrolled_count = 50, reached_count = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of retention_pct.
questions.a: 720 per cent

questions.q: Compute the survival rate of an enrolled batch from the two counts. Use the method 'School Retention Rate'. Work with: enrolled_count = 200, reached_count = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of retention_pct.
questions.a: 120 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'School Retention Rate' refers to.
questions.a: The share of enrolled children who stay the course to a later standard is the still enrolled count expressed as a percentage of the intake -- the survival measure behind the finding that only about a third of Standard I entrants reach Standard VIII.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'School Retention Rate'.
questions.a: A little over one in three entrants survives to Standard VIII, so the rest drop out along the way.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'School Retention Rate', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: retention_pct = reached_count / enrolled_count * 100
